papers.title: Human amniotic mesenchymal stem cell-derived exosomes alleviate cerebral Palsy-Associated neuronal damage via TSC1/mTOR/ULK1 autophagy suppression and PINK1/Parkin mitophagy restoration.
papers.summary: This study looks at how exosomes (tiny secreted vesicles) from human amniotic mesenchymal stem cells can help protect neurons damaged in a cerebral palsy model. The researchers found that these exosomes work by calming down excessive autophagy (the cell's self-degradation process) through the TSC1/mTOR/ULK1 pathway, while also restoring proper mitophagy (selective clearance of damaged mitochondria) via the PINK1/Parkin pathway. The net effect is reduced neuronal damage, suggesting a therapeutic strategy for cerebral palsy based on rebalancing these two cellular quality-control systems.
papers.why: This paper directly addresses the molecular crosstalk between autophagy and mitophagy regulation in neurons, offering mechanistic insight (TSC1/mTOR/ULK1 and PINK1/Parkin pathways) that could inform how these pathways are studied or targeted in other neuronal contexts relevant to the PhD project.

papers.title: Intercellular Mitochondrial Transfer in Parkinson's Disease: Cargo Quality, Cell State Vulnerability, and Therapeutic Selectivity.
papers.summary: This paper discusses how mitochondria can be transferred between cells in Parkinson's disease, highlighting that the quality of the transferred mitochondrial cargo matters for whether it helps or harms recipient cells. It explores how different cellular states affect vulnerability to dysfunctional mitochondria, and suggests that therapies could be designed to selectively promote healthy mitochondrial transfer while blocking harmful transfer. The work frames intercellular mitochondrial transfer as both a disease mechanism and a potential therapeutic target in neurodegeneration.
papers.why: Understanding how mitochondrial quality and intercellular transfer influence neuronal vulnerability is directly relevant to mitophagy and mitochondrial quality control in neurons, a core theme of this PhD project on neurodegeneration.

papers.title: Rescue from the bottom of the (beta) barrel: Outer mitochondrial membrane quality control.
papers.summary: This paper discusses how cells monitor and repair the outer mitochondrial membrane, focusing on quality control mechanisms for beta-barrel proteins embedded in that membrane. It likely covers how misfolded or damaged beta-barrel proteins are detected and either rescued or degraded to maintain mitochondrial integrity. This connects to broader themes of mitochondrial surveillance systems that work alongside mitophagy to preserve organelle health.
papers.why: Outer mitochondrial membrane quality control mechanisms are a key upstream determinant of whether damaged mitochondria are tagged for mitophagy, directly relevant to understanding neuronal mitochondrial turnover in the brain.

papers.title: Histology-guided spatial metabolomics integrated with multi-omics and cellular validation maps renal metabolic heterogeneity in ochratoxin A-induced nephrotoxicity.
papers.summary: This paper uses histology-guided spatial metabolomics combined with other omics data to study how ochratoxin A, a toxic compound, damages kidney tissue. The researchers mapped out which metabolic changes occur in specific regions of the kidney and validated findings using cellular experiments. The result is a detailed spatial picture of how kidney toxicity develops at the molecular level across different tissue zones.
papers.why: While focused on kidney rather than brain tissue, this paper demonstrates a histology-guided spatial metabolomics workflow integrated with multi-omics and cellular validation that could serve as a methodological template for mapping metabolic heterogeneity in neuronal tissue, including perineuronal net regions.

papers.title: Targeting SIRT6 to regulate mitophagy: A novel strategy to combat senescence in osteoarthritic chondrocytes.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how SIRT6, a protein involved in cell regulation, controls mitophagy (the clearance of damaged mitochondria) in cartilage cells called chondrocytes. The researchers propose that boosting SIRT6 activity could reduce cellular senescence (aging-related cell dysfunction) that contributes to osteoarthritis. The work suggests a potential therapeutic strategy targeting mitochondrial quality control to slow joint disease progression.
papers.why: While this study focuses on cartilage rather than neurons, the core mechanism of SIRT6-regulated mitophagy controlling cellular senescence could offer conceptual insights transferable to understanding mitophagy dysregulation in aging neurons and interneurons.

papers.title: FUNDC1-Mediated Mitophagy in Cardiovascular Disease: Context-Dependent Regulation of Mitochondrial Quality Control and Dysfunction.
papers.summary: This paper reviews FUNDC1, a mitophagy receptor that tags damaged mitochondria for clearance, and how its regulation shifts depending on cellular context in cardiovascular disease. It discusses how FUNDC1 activity can be protective in some settings but harmful in others, depending on stress type and disease stage. The review likely covers upstream signaling, post-translational modifications, and how dysregulated FUNDC1-mediated mitophagy contributes to mitochondrial dysfunction in the heart and vasculature.
papers.why: Although focused on cardiovascular tissue, this paper provides mechanistic detail on FUNDC1-mediated mitophagy regulation that could inform how similar pathways are interpreted in neurons and interneurons within your mitophagy-focused project.

papers.title: Epigenetic and Post-Transcriptional Regulation of Autophagy in Inflammatory Bowel Disease.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how autophagy, the cellular process of self-degradation and recycling, is regulated by epigenetic mechanisms (like DNA methylation and histone modifications) and post-transcriptional controls (like microRNAs) in inflammatory bowel disease. It discusses how these regulatory layers affect autophagy gene expression in gut tissue during inflammation. The focus is on intestinal epithelial and immune cells rather than neurons or brain tissue.
papers.why: This paper's relevance is limited since it concerns autophagy regulation in gut inflammation rather than neuronal mitophagy or brain tissue, though the epigenetic/post-transcriptional regulatory mechanisms discussed could offer conceptual parallels for autophagy regulation in interneurons.
